description: Two-panel tensile-property figure for a Fe–10Mn–10Al–0.7C low-density steel annealed for 1 h at eight temperatures. (a) Engineering stress–engineering strain curves; x-axis "Engineering Strain" 0.0–0.4 (0.1 ticks), y-axis "Engineering Stress (MPa)" 0–1200 (200 MPa ticks). Eight colour-coded curves are labelled both in-plot and in the legend as 700 °C, 1 h; 800 °C, 1 h; 850 °C, 1 h; 900 °C, 1 h; 950 °C, 1 h; 1000 °C, 1 h; 1100 °C, 1 h; 1200 °C, 1 h. Curves for higher annealing temperatures generally lie below those for lower temperatures; the 700 °C curve rises highest (between the 800 and 1000 MPa gridlines) while 900 °C extends furthest in strain (past 0.3). (b) Overlay of true stress–true strain and work hardening rate curves; x-axis "True Strain" 0.00–0.35 (0.05 ticks), y-axis "True Stress / Work Hardening Rate (MPa)" 0–6000 (1000 MPa ticks). Two curve families are superimposed: steeply falling work hardening rate curves starting near 6000 MPa and decaying to ~1000 MPa, and low-lying true stress curves confined below ~1000 MPa; some curves end abruptly where the specimen fractured. The figure demonstrates the strength–ductility trade-off with annealing temperature and the crossover in early-stage work-hardening behaviour between κ-carbide-bearing (700–850 °C) and κ-carbide-free (≥900 °C) conditions.

subfigures.description: Engineering stress–engineering strain curves (x: Engineering Strain 0.0–0.4; y: Engineering Stress, MPa, 0–1200; 200 MPa ticks) for the eight annealed conditions; each curve carries an in-plot temperature label and a matching legend entry ('700 °C, 1 h' … '1200 °C, 1 h'). Higher annealing temperature gives a lower-lying curve; the 700 °C, 1 h curve is highest and the 900 °C, 1 h curve reaches the largest engineering strain.

Combined true stress–true strain and work hardening rate plot (x: True Strain 0.00–0.35; y: True Stress / Work Hardening Rate, MPa, 0–6000; 1000 MPa ticks). Eight work hardening rate curves fall steeply from near 6000 MPa at low true strain toward ~1000 MPa, while the true stress curves form a separate low band below ~1000 MPa; several curves terminate abruptly at different true strains (earlier fracture for some conditions). Labels 700 °C to 1200 °C with arrows point to the corresponding curves.

observations.observation: Panel (a) is an engineering stress–engineering strain plot with axes Engineering Stress (MPa), 0–1200 in 200 MPa steps, and Engineering Strain, 0.0–0.4 in 0.1 steps, containing eight curves labelled 700 °C through 1200 °C (1 h).

In panel (a) the curve of each higher annealing temperature lies below the curve of the next lower annealing temperature, so the 700 °C curve is the highest and the 1200 °C curve the lowest (engineering stress at a given strain).

In panel (a) the 700 °C, 1 h curve peaks above the 800 MPa gridline (between 800 and 1000 MPa) but at a small strain, whereas the 900 °C, 1 h curve reaches the largest engineering strain, extending beyond the 0.3 gridline.

Panel (b) plots two quantities on one axis, 'True Stress / Work Hardening Rate (MPa)' from 0 to 6000 (1000 MPa ticks) against 'True Strain' 0.00–0.35; the steeply decaying curves reach ~6000 MPa at the lowest true strain, while the true stress curves stay below about 1000 MPa.
In panel (b) several of the true stress curves terminate abruptly at different true strains, indicating earlier fracture/snapping of some annealed conditions.
The caption states that (a) shows engineering stress–engineering strain curves of the annealed specimens and (b) shows the true stress–true strain curves together with work hardening rate curves.

The citing text states that the annealed specimens show continuous yielding except the specimen annealed at 700 °C, and that for the 700 °C specimen the work hardening rate curve is calculated only after the yielding period.

The citing text states that for specimens annealed at 700 °C, 800 °C and 850 °C (with κ-carbide distributed in the α or γ matrix) the work hardening rates are in the reverse order of the annealing temperatures when true strain is less than about 5%.

The citing text states that for specimens annealed at or over 900 °C (no obvious κ-carbide in the α or γ matrix) the work hardening rates are lower than those of the 700 °C, 800 °C and 850 °C specimens when true strain is less than about 5%.
The citing text states that the 900 °C and 950 °C specimens possess similar work hardening rates, while the specimen annealed at 950 °C snapped earlier.

The citing text reports that after annealing at 900 °C for 1 h the ultimate strength is 855 MPa, the yield strength 651 MPa, the ultimate elongation 36.6% and the product of strength and ductility 31 GPa%; these numeric values are given in text/Table 1, not printed on the curves of Fig. 15.

The citing text states that specimens annealed at 700 °C, 800 °C and 850 °C bear a high work hardening rate at the early stage but their work hardening rates decrease quickly until failure occurs, and that the 850 °C specimen's work hardening rate falls below that of the 900 °C specimen at higher strain.

unreadable_items: panel (b): the eight work hardening rate curves overlap heavily at true strain below ~0.02 so the per-condition colour assignment in that region cannot be resolved reliably from the pixels alone
no numerical values are printed on any curve in (a) or (b); only axis ticks are readable
